# Mahārāhulovāda Sutta (MN 62 (PTS MN i 420))

**ID:** MN 62 (PTS MN i 420)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Mahārāhulovāda Sutta
**PTS:** MN i 420
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahārāhulovāda Sutta* (MN 62; PTS MN i 420–426) is the sixty-second discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya*, set at Jeta's Grove near Sāvatthi [Lamotte 1988; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The sutta begins while the Buddha and his son Rāhula are going for alms; the Buddha instructs Rāhula to contemplate all material form—past, present, or future, internal or external—as not-self ("not mine, not I, not my self") [Radich 2007]. After Sāriputta separately advises Rāhula to practice mindfulness of breathing, Rāhula approaches the Buddha for instruction. The Buddha presents a broad meditative curriculum prior to breath contemplation: Rāhula is taught to contemplate the internal and external physical elements (earth, water, fire, wind, and space), using them as metaphors to cultivate endurance and impartiality without aversion or attachment [Polak 2011; Anālayo 2016; Tzungkuen Wen]. This is followed by the cultivation of the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), the perception of unattractiveness (*asubha*), and the perception of impermanence (*anicca*) [Anālayo 2016]. Finally, the Buddha details the complete sixteen-step scheme of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*), declaring that its mastery ensures mindful awareness even of one's final breaths [Anālayo 2016; Anālayo 2019].

Curated parallels include *Ekottarika-āgama* discourse EĀ 17.1, chapter 20 of the *Arthaviniścaya*, *Saṁyutta Nikāya* 54.1, *Saṁyuktāgama* parallels (SĀ 803, SĀ 815, SĀ³ 15), Sanskrit fragments (SHT sutta 84), and Vinaya *Pārājika* 3 [Lamotte 1988; Anālayo 2019]. As noted by Anālayo, EĀ 17.1 preserves only the initial three steps of the sixteen-step breathing formula due to text corruption and reworking [Anālayo 2019].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels: EA 17.1 羅雲
- Passage-level parallels: SN 54.1 Ekadhammasutta; MN 118 (PTS MN iii 78) Ānāpānassati Sutta; Bu-Vb Pj3 Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pārājika 3; SA 803 一明
- Resembling parallels: Arv 20 Ṣoḍaśākārā Ānāpāna-Smṛtiḥ; SA3 15 一明; SA 815 布薩; SHT Sutta 84
- Mentioned in: Mil 7.4.6 Ākāsaṅgapañha; Mil 7.4.3 Tejaṅgapañha

**Sources**

- [Lamotte 1988] Etienne Lamotte, History of Indian Buddhism (1988) — Distinguished the text from MN 61 and identified its Ekottarika-āgama correspondence.
- [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995] Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Middle Length Discourses of the Buddha (1995) — Provided English title, geographic setting at Sāvatthi, and discourse outline.
- [Anālayo 2016] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Mindfully Facing Disease and Death (2016) — Detailed the meditative sequence: elements, divine abodes, unattractiveness, impermanence, and the 16 steps of breath meditation.
- [Anālayo 2019] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Mindfulness of Breathing: A Practice Guide and Translations (2019) — Analyzed the EĀ parallel and the proclamation regarding awareness of one's final breaths.
- [Polak 2011] Grzegorz Polak, Reexamining Jhana (2011) — Noted the five elements used as metaphors for mental qualities and the ānāpānasati formula.
- [Radich 2007] Michael David Radich, The Somatics of Liberation (2007) — Discussed textual stratification, de-identification formulas, and bodily element analysis.
- [Tzungkuen Wen] Tzungkuen Wen, A Study of Sukkhavipassaka in Pali Buddhism — Discussed the division into internal and external elements in MN 62 alongside MN 28 and MN 140.
